newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Chirac flies in to frosty welcome in Israel.
newsitem.headline: Chirac flies in to frosty welcome in Israel.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac arrived in Israel on Monday to a cool welcome from a hardline government that bluntly rejects his bid for a European role as co-sponsor of the Middle East peace process.

Chirac's visit was preceded by a series of diplomatic incidents that bared raw feelings on both sides about France's "Arab policy" and Israel's rejection of any further territorial concession to its Arab neighbours.

Israeli media gave little prominence to his visit, but the English-language Jerusalem Post, which often reflects right-wing government thinking, greeted him with a vitriolic editorial as a "biased would-be broker" who showed "fawning support of the region's most unregenerate terrorist states".

"If ever there were a state which disqualified itself from the role of an honest broker, France is it," the paper said. "France remains a rabid partisan -- and as such, it has no place in the Middle East peace talks."
At a welcoming ceremony with President Ezer Weizman in the presence of hardline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Chirac called himself a friend of Israel.
"This friend comes to you at a time when your region is going through a difficult period," he said. "But I know that the Israel people aspire to peace, as do its leaders."

Weizman referred obliquely to Israeli claims to sovereignty over the whole of Jerusalem, which France and most of the international community do not recognise, by welcoming Chirac to "Jerusalem, capital of our nation".

Arriving directly from two days of talks with President Hafez al-Assad in Syria, where he was given a hero's welcome, Chirac said he was convinced all the peoples and governments of the Middle East wanted peace in their own way.
But even before he reached Jerusalem, Netanyahu had brushed aside France's call for a political role for the European Union, the main aid donor to the region, in Arab-Israeli negotiations.
"I would be very careful before I would add more cooks to the broth," Netanyahu said. "I don't think at this time in such sensitive negotiations it would be wise to introduce another interlocutor."

U.S. special envoy Dennis Ross, who has been trying to broker a deal on an Israeli troop withdrawal from the West Bank city of Hebron, threatened to go home on Monday out of frustration at the deadlock, PLO and diplomatic sources said.
By a symbolic coincidence, Chirac's plane parked close to Ross's U.S. government jet on the tarmac at Ben Gurion airport.

While Chirac reviewed an honour guard with Weizman, his junior health minister, Herve Gaymard, was visiting a disputed PLO headquarters in Arab East Jerusalem to meet Faisal al- Husseini, leading PLO official in the city.

France decided its foreign minister would boycott the Israel leg of Chirac's trip after the Israelis refused to let him visit Orient House, which the Netanyahu administration says violates Israel-PLO peace accords.
On Sunday, Chirac toned down his call for an EU peace role, telling a news conference: "I did not come here to teach people lessons...Naturally we are not trying to force our way in.
"I am simply saying that we are available and we have valid reasons to be involved, and that a certain balance of things may justify the presence of Europe and of France."

Chirac planned to give his keynote speech in Israel at the Haifa Technion institute later on Monday before attending a state dinner with Weizman. He will hold talks with Netanyahu on Tuesday after touring the Old City of Arab East Jerusalem.
